patient.chief_complaint: Acute right-sided weakness, headache, and nausea for 1 day
patient.history_present_illness: A 28-year-old previously healthy right-handed Hispanic woman presents to the emergency department with a 1-day history of progressive right-sided weakness, severe headache, and nausea with one episode of vomiting. She reports that the symptoms began yesterday morning upon awakening, initially noticing difficulty gripping her coffee mug with her right hand. Over the course of the day, she developed a progressively worsening holocephalic headache rated 8/10 in severity, accompanied by nausea and photophobia. By the evening, she noted difficulty walking due to weakness in her right leg, prompting her partner to bring her to the emergency department. She denies any preceding febrile illness, recent travel, insect bites, or trauma. She has no prior history of neurological symptoms, seizures, or similar episodes. She was seen by her primary care physician 6 months ago for a routine physical and was in good health. Of note, her father was diagnosed with glioblastoma at age 52 and passed away two years ago, which is causing her significant anxiety about the possibility of a brain tumor. She denies any recent weight loss, night sweats, or changes in appetite. She reports no visual changes, speech difficulties, or sensory symptoms. She has been taking combined oral contraceptives for the past 3 years without complications. On initial assessment in the emergency department, she was hemodynamically stable with mild tachycardia. Neurological examination was notable for right hemiparesis, a right Babinski sign, and bilateral papilledema.

results.title: Tumefactive Demyelinating Lesions: Conventional and Advanced MRI Features
results.authors: Lucchinetti CF, Gavrilova RH, Metz I, et al.
results.summary: Tumefactive demyelinating lesions (>2 cm) can mimic brain neoplasms. Key MRI features favoring demyelination include: open-ring (incomplete) enhancement, leading-edge restricted diffusion, and relatively low rCBV on perfusion imaging compared to gliomas.

results.title: Distinguishing tumefactive demyelinating lesions from CNS neoplasm: MR spectroscopy and perfusion
results.authors: Kiriyama T, Kataoka H, Kasai T, et al.
results.summary: MRS in tumefactive MS may show elevated choline and decreased NAA similar to gliomas, making spectroscopy alone insufficient for diagnosis. However, elevated myo-inositol and glutamate/glutamine ratios favor demyelination. Perfusion showing rCBV <1.75 supports demyelination.

results.title: Tumefactive demyelinating lesions: an uncommon diagnostic challenge
results.summary: Tumefactive MS is defined as demyelinating lesions >2 cm with mass effect, edema, and/or ring enhancement. May occur as the first demyelinating event. Biopsy should be interpreted cautiously as reactive changes can mimic low-grade glioma. Absence of OCBs occurs in 5-10% of MS patients.

output.proposed: Methylprednisolone 1g IV daily for 5 days (pulse corticosteroid therapy for tumefactive MS)
interactions: Oral contraceptives: corticosteroids may reduce efficacy of hormonal contraception; counsel patient regarding backup contraception
Ibuprofen: increased risk of GI ulceration and bleeding with concurrent corticosteroid and NSAID use
warnings: Monitor blood glucose closely during high-dose corticosteroid therapy
Consider GI prophylaxis with proton pump inhibitor during pulse steroid course
Psychiatric side effects (insomnia, agitation, psychosis) can occur with high-dose IV methylprednisolone
Taper should be individualized; abrupt discontinuation after prolonged use may cause adrenal crisis
alternatives: Plasma exchange (PLEX) if corticosteroid response is inadequate
IV immunoglobulin (IVIG) as second-line if PLEX not available

output.interpretation: Bland CSF profile: minimal lymphocytic activity, normal protein and glucose, intact blood-brain barrier, no oligoclonal bands, normal IgG index and synthesis rate. Cytology and flow cytometry without malignant or clonal populations. Infectious workup negative. AQP4 and MOG antibodies negative. The CSF does not support an inflammatory demyelinating, infectious, or neoplastic process by itself; results are non-discriminating between high-grade glioma and an atypical demyelinating lesion. Note: absent oligoclonal bands does not exclude MS — a minority of demyelinating cases (5–10%) are OCB-negative.

differential.key_features: Homogeneous enhancement (often without open ring), periventricular location, restricted diffusion, marked steroid sensitivity; consider in immunocompromised hosts — distinguish by biopsy if imaging is equivocal
Closed-ring enhancement (rather than open ring with cortical-side break), elevated choline:NAA on spectroscopy, lack of CSF oligoclonal bands; tissue diagnosis often required
AQP4-IgG positivity, longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis, area postrema syndrome — must be excluded before DMT selection
MOG-IgG positivity, ADEM-like large lesions especially in younger patients, frequent lesion resolution on follow-up MRI
Restricted diffusion centrally (not peripheral), thick smooth ring, fever and elevated inflammatory markers, predisposing source (dental, sinus, endocarditis)
Monophasic, post-infectious/post-vaccination, encephalopathy hallmark; large confluent lesions; MOG-IgG sometimes positive in young adults

optimal_actions.action: Obtain contrast-enhanced brain MRI with MS protocol (FLAIR, T2, DWI, pre- and post-gadolinium T1) to assess dissemination in space and time
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Multifocal T2/FLAIR hyperintensities in MS-typical regions (periventricular, juxtacortical/cortical, infratentorial); presence of gadolinium-enhancing lesion(s) supports dissemination in time when also non-enhancing lesions present

optimal_actions.action: Extend MRI to cervical and thoracic spinal cord with contrast — ~80% of MS patients have cord lesions, and cord involvement counts toward dissemination in space
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Short-segment (<2 vertebral bodies) peripheral cord lesions favor MS over NMOSD (which characteristically shows longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis ≥3 segments)

optimal_actions.action: Perform lumbar puncture for CSF analysis including oligoclonal bands (paired serum), IgG index, cell count, protein, and glucose — defer until mass effect resolves
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Lumbar puncture is supportive but must be deferred until brain MRI confirms no significant mass effect or impending herniation; in this case the mass-effect imaging features make LP relatively contraindicated until cytoreductive treatment or steroid response is established

optimal_actions.action: Order broad mimic-exclusion serology: CBC, CMP, TSH, vitamin B12, vitamin D, ANA, AQP4-IgG (cell-based assay), MOG-IgG (cell-based assay), HIV, and RPR
optimal_actions.expected_finding: AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG negative; B12, TSH, HIV, RPR normal — excludes NMOSD, MOGAD, B12 deficiency, thyroid disease, neurosyphilis, and HIV-associated demyelination

optimal_actions.expected_finding: Retrieves McDonald 2017 criteria and contemporary DMT guidance (platform vs. high-efficacy choice, NEDA-3 outcome framework)

useless_tools.rationale: EEG has no role in MS diagnosis — findings are non-specific and do not contribute to dissemination in space or time.
CT is markedly inferior to MRI for visualising demyelinating plaques; ordering CT delays diagnosis and adds radiation without clinical benefit.
No cardiac indication in a typical MS workup; echocardiography does not inform the demyelinating differential.
Cardiac monitoring is only indicated for first-dose fingolimod initiation (bradyarrhythmia risk) — not as part of MS diagnostic workup.
FDG-PET is not indicated for MS diagnosis or DMT decisions; it does not differentiate demyelination from mimics and adds substantial cost.

sequence_constraints.reason: Brain MRI must precede lumbar puncture to exclude significant mass effect, midline shift, or impending herniation — in this case mass-effect features make LP without prior imaging a safety event

critical_actions: Establish dissemination in space (DIS) using brain and spinal-cord MRI in MS-typical regions (periventricular, juxtacortical/cortical, infratentorial, spinal cord)
Establish dissemination in time (DIT) by demonstrating simultaneous enhancing and non-enhancing lesions, a new lesion on follow-up MRI, or CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands (per McDonald 2017)
Exclude NMOSD and MOGAD with AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG cell-based assays before committing to an MS diagnosis and DMT
Order CSF analysis with paired serum to assess oligoclonal bands and IgG index
For tumefactive presentations with mass effect, consult neurosurgery and consider brain biopsy if imaging plus CSF/serology do not establish diagnosis with confidence
Treat the acute relapse with high-dose IV methylprednisolone (1 g daily for 3–5 days), with plasma exchange reserved for steroid-refractory severe relapses
Initiate a disease-modifying therapy (DMT) after relapse stabilization; choice between platform vs. high-efficacy agent based on disease activity, MRI burden, and patient preference
Check JC virus antibody serostatus before considering natalizumab; verify up-to-date vaccinations (especially live-attenuated) before initiating B-cell depleting or S1P-modulator DMTs
Counsel on Uhthoff phenomenon, heat avoidance, smoking cessation, and vitamin D supplementation as modifiable lifestyle factors
contraindicated_actions: Do not perform lumbar puncture before brain MRI confirms absence of significant mass effect / midline shift / impending herniation — features in this case (mass effect, midline shift, or papilledema) make LP a safety event without prior imaging clearance
Do not diagnose MS based on non-specific white-matter lesions alone without meeting McDonald 2017 criteria and excluding mimics
Do not start natalizumab in a JC virus-antibody-positive patient (especially with high index) without explicit benefit-risk discussion of PML
Do not initiate fingolimod without a baseline ECG and first-dose bradyarrhythmia monitoring; avoid in patients with second-degree AV block, prior MI, or severe sleep apnea
Do not start teriflunomide in a woman of child-bearing potential without effective contraception (teratogenic, long elimination half-life)
Do not use chronic oral corticosteroids as a maintenance treatment for MS — they are ineffective long-term and carry significant harm
Do not administer live-attenuated vaccines after initiation of B-cell depleting therapy (ocrelizumab, ofatumumab) or S1P modulators (fingolimod, ozanimod)
Do not omit spinal-cord MRI in a patient with myelopathic signs even if the brain MRI alone meets DIS criteria — cord lesions change relapse counting and management

Do not pursue aggressive cytoreductive surgery for a presumed tumefactive demyelinating lesion before exhausting non-invasive workup — open ring enhancement, CSF OCBs, and AQP4/MOG serology should be obtained first
key_reasoning_points: MS is a clinical-radiographic diagnosis: McDonald 2017 requires dissemination in space (DIS) and dissemination in time (DIT) plus exclusion of better explanations — no single test confirms it

MS-typical MRI regions are periventricular, juxtacortical/cortical, infratentorial, and spinal cord — recognising a lesion in three of these regions establishes DIS for an attack-meeting clinical event
CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands (≥2 bands not present in paired serum) can substitute for DIT under McDonald 2017 when DIS is met — this changes the calculus for clinically isolated syndromes

Short-segment (<2 vertebral bodies), peripheral, dorsolateral or dorsal-column spinal cord lesions strongly favour MS over NMOSD (which characteristically produces longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis ≥3 segments)

Tumefactive demyelinating lesions are a recognised MS variant — distinguishing imaging features from neoplasm include open ring enhancement, prominent intralesional venules, less mass effect than expected for size, and CSF OCBs; brain biopsy should be a last resort
Open-ring enhancement with the opening oriented toward the cortex is a high-specificity sign of demyelination, distinguishing tumefactive MS from neoplasm and abscess
AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG must be ordered as cell-based assays, not ELISA — the older ELISA-based AQP4 assays have unacceptable false-negative rates
T1 hypointense 'black holes' indicate axonal loss from prior inflammatory episodes and contribute evidence of dissemination in time even without simultaneous enhancing lesions

Choice of DMT — platform agent (interferon-β, glatiramer, teriflunomide, dimethyl fumarate) vs. high-efficacy agent (natalizumab, ocrelizumab, ofatumumab, cladribine, S1P modulators) — should weigh disease activity, MRI burden, patient comorbidities, JCV serostatus, and reproductive plans
If the initial brain MRI does not include the spinal cord, extending imaging to cervical and thoracic cord is essential — both for diagnostic DIS and for relapse counting

metadata.difficulty_description: Initial presentation mimics high-grade glioma with large ring-enhancing lesion, mass effect, and a family history of GBM as a strong red herring. CSF lacks typical MS markers (no oligoclonal bands, normal IgG index). MRS findings overlap with neoplasm. The correct diagnosis requires recognizing subtle imaging features (open-ring enhancement, leading-edge diffusion restriction), pursuing tissue diagnosis, and integrating findings from multiple modalities including a small contralateral periventricular lesion that hints at multifocal demyelination.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Tumefactive demyelinating lesion overlaps imaging features with neoplasm/abscess; differential must include CNS lymphoma and high-grade glioma; agent must integrate open-ring enhancement, CSF OCB status, and AQP4/MOG serology to avoid biopsy
